c1.story:
Every weekday evening in Bengaluru, as the traffic on Outer Ring Road finally crawls home, a second shift is just logging in. Their bosses are in New Jersey, their clients in Charlotte and Frankfurt, and the systems they keep alive move money, ship parcels and settle insurance claims for people who will never know an Indian engineer touched them. That is the Indian IT industry: the back office, and increasingly the engine room, of Western corporations.

It began with a deadline. In the late nineties the world panicked that its computers would misread the year 2000, and American companies needed armies of programmers to fix old code fast and cheap. TCS, Infosys and Wipro supplied them, proved the model worked, and spent the next two decades moving from patching code to running entire technology estates. Today the sector looks like one thing from a distance and four things up close.

The first door holds the giants, TCS, Infosys, HCLTech and Wipro, with multi-year contracts to run and modernise the technology of the world's largest companies. The second holds the mid-cap specialists such as Coforge, Mphasis and Hexaware, which go deep in one or two industries, insurance or banking say, and steal deals the giants find too small or too fiddly. The third designs products rather than running IT: L&T Technology Services and Tata Technologies work on car electronics, aircraft parts and medical devices. The fourth, Netweb, CP Plus, STL and ITI, sells physical things: servers, cameras, optical fibre and telecom gear, mostly to Indian buyers.

Three doors earn dollars from Western budgets. The fourth earns rupees from Indian capex. Do not put them in one basket.

Why does the door matter? Because the same headline lands differently on each. A US bank cutting its technology budget hits the giants first. A European carmaker delaying a new model hits engineering services. A government data-centre push helps the hardware names and does nothing for Infosys. Most of the listed value sits behind the first door, which is why the Nifty IT index moves with American and European boardrooms far more than with anything happening in India.
c1.read:
Four tiles, four doors. Read each from top to bottom, then compare the bars across them.

  • The name and the line under it say what the company actually sells and how it bills: multi-year run-and-modernise contracts in dollars and euros, deep industry niches, product design work, or boxes of hardware.
  • The tickers are listed names that mostly live behind that door; click one to open its stock page. The first tile carries the four biggest names in the sector, which is where most of the market value sits.
  • The profit bar shows how much of each sale the company gets to keep. The giants sit at high: scale, net cash and a pyramid of young engineers let them hold a fat operating margin. Mid caps and engineering services sit at medium, because they spend more to win business and lean on fewer clients. Hardware sits at low: it buys components, fights on tenders and carries inventory, the opposite of an asset-light model.
  • The last line is the bet. Read the first tile's carefully: it is not only about tech budgets but about staying the cheapest safe pair of hands as AI changes the work.

Below the tiles, the catering analogy maps each door to a kind of kitchen business, and the so-what line gives the practical rule: the fourth door belongs in a different mental basket. If you hold an IT fund, check how much of it is hardware before blaming, or crediting, AI for its returns.

c2.story:
Picture the industry as a relay race across two continents. The baton starts in an engineering college in Tiruchirappalli or Warangal, where a fresh graduate signs an offer letter. It passes to a training campus, the most famous being Infosys's sprawling one in Mysuru, where she learns the company's way of writing and testing code. Then she sits down in a delivery centre in Pune or Hyderabad, at a desk whose hours are billed to a client she may never meet.

The third leg is the one outsiders forget. Almost nothing Indian IT builds is built from scratch. It sits on platforms owned by others: Microsoft's and Amazon's clouds, Salesforce, SAP, and now the AI models of OpenAI and Anthropic. Indian firms are the contractors who know how to install, connect and run those platforms inside a messy, decades-old bank. That makes them partners of the American platforms and, quietly, dependent on them.

The fourth leg is the sale. An account manager in New York or London renews a multi-year contract with the client's technology chief, competing head on against Accenture, the Dublin-headquartered consulting giant, and Cognizant, the New Jersey firm whose engineers mostly sit in Chennai and Bengaluru. And increasingly the client asks a pointed question: why not do this ourselves? Global firms now run their own captive centres in India, hiring the same engineers from the same colleges.

The whole race runs on one gap. Revenue is earned in dollars and euros, at the final leg. Cost is paid in rupees, at the first two legs. That is why a weaker rupee feels like a pay rise for the company, and why a US visa rule, which raises the cost of putting engineers at the client's site, goes straight to the margin.

Revenue is decided in New York and London. Cost is decided in Bengaluru. The margin lives in the exchange rate between them.
c2.read:
Read the five boxes left to right: that is the journey of one engineer's hour, from college to client invoice.

  • Talent is the raw material: graduates, trained in-house and paid in rupees.
  • Delivery centres is where the listed Indian names stand, the giants and the mid caps crowded into one box. This is their home turf.
  • Platforms and partners belongs to the American tech giants and AI labs. Indian firms build on top; they do not own it.
  • Client relationship is the sales station, and the one with a named rival standing in it.
  • End client is the Western company paying the bills.

Now drop to the band row underneath. The coloured cell marked India listed sits under exactly one station, the second. Everything to its right belongs to someone else: platforms to US tech, the relationship contested by Accenture and Cognizant, the budget to the client. That is the sector's position in one glance: excellent at delivery, dependent on others for the platform and the purse.

The rival band sits on the relationship station, which tells you where competition really happens: not on the cost of an engineer, where India wins, but on whom the client's technology chief trusts. Captive centres, named alongside the rivals, compete for the same trust from inside the client.

The geography note gives you the money map: roughly six in ten rupees of revenue from North America, a quarter from Europe, almost all cost in Indian salaries. Use it like this: news at the right end of the diagram is a revenue story; news at the left end is a margin story.

c3.story:
If you want to know what Indian IT will report next quarter, do not start with Indian IT. Start with JPMorgan, Citi and Bank of America. Banking and financial services is the largest customer group for almost every large cap, and the technology budgets those banks set this quarter show up as Indian revenue the next.

Banks buy everything: core banking systems, payment rails, compliance tooling, cloud migration, whole operations floors outsourced to Chennai. But they buy two kinds of work, and the difference between them is the cycle. Run-the-bank work, keeping old systems alive, is sticky, boring and survives recessions. Change-the-bank work, new apps and new platforms, the discretionary projects, is what gets cut first when profits wobble or rates rise. In March 2023, when Silicon Valley Bank collapsed in a couple of days, American banks did not stop running their systems. They froze the shiny new projects, and Indian IT growth sank to low single digits within a few quarters.

Run-the-bank work pays the rent. Change-the-bank work pays for the re-rating.

The other tiles follow their own clocks. Insurers buy modernisation of policy and claims systems, some still running on mainframes older than the engineers maintaining them, and they buy it hardest during cost-cutting drives, which makes them a usefully counter-cyclical client. Retailers buy e-commerce and supply-chain technology and move with the American shopper and, since 2025, with tariffs. Carmakers buy engineering design and embedded software, so the electric-vehicle cycle and Europe's struggling auto industry decide a large part of engineering services revenue. Healthcare follows US policy and pharma research budgets. Hi-tech clients follow their own hiring and funding.

And then there is the odd tile out: the Indian government and Indian enterprises, buying servers, cameras, telecom gear and digital public infrastructure. That tile feeds the fourth door almost alone, and it moves with Delhi's capex, not Manhattan's.
c3.read:
Eight tiles, eight customer groups. Each has three lines: who buys, what they buy, and what moves them. The third line is your watch list outside India.

Start with the first tile, banks and financial services. It comes first because it is the biggest client for nearly every large cap, and its third line, US bank profits, rates and regulation, is the most useful single thing to track. The so-what line under the grid says it plainly: US bank earnings calls are a quarter-early read on Indian IT.

Then group the tiles by what drives them:

  • Rate and profit sensitive: banks, insurers, and hi-tech and software companies. These swing hardest with US interest rates and corporate profits.
  • Consumer and trade sensitive: retail and consumer goods, which now carry a tariff line.
  • Industrial: manufacturing and autos, telecom and media, which follow capex cycles and Europe's economy. Engineering services lives here.
  • Policy driven: healthcare, which moves with US healthcare policy, and the Indian government tile, which moves with Indian capex.

Now cross-check with card one. The large caps sell into almost every tile, which makes them diversified but tied to the US economy as a whole. Mid caps often lean on one or two tiles, insurance or banking. Engineering services leans on the manufacturing tile, and the hardware door on the last tile. A company's revenue split by vertical, disclosed every quarter in its fact sheet, tells you which third lines to watch for that name.

c4.story:
Strip an Indian IT company to its bones and you find a manpower agency with very good manners. It hires engineers, pays them in rupees, and bills their time to clients in dollars. Salaries and subcontractors eat more than half of every rupee of revenue. Offices, laptops and interest barely register. So the profit and loss statement is really a story about people: how many you have, how many are billed, how senior they are, and what the rupee did this quarter.

Take utilisation first. An engineer on the bench, hired but not billed, is pure cost. Push up the share of billed engineers and margins rise without a single price increase. Then the pyramid: a project staffed with many juniors under a few seniors costs far less than one run by veterans, while the client pays much the same blended rate. In 2022, when attrition topped a fifth and companies poached seniors with double-digit raises, the pyramid got top-heavy and margins shrank even as revenue boomed. In the bust that followed, attrition fell, wage hikes shrank, the bench was trimmed, and margins recovered while revenue stalled.

Then the rupee. Because revenue is in dollars and cost in rupees, a weaker rupee widens margin almost one for one. It is the closest thing this industry has to free money, and it explains why IT earnings held up better than IT revenue through 2024 and 2025.

In IT, margin up with growth flat is usually the rupee or a hiring freeze, not a better business.

The quieter line is receivables. Clients pay late, and some work is done but not yet billed. Days of sales outstanding creeping up is the first sign of a client in trouble or a project in dispute, and it shows up before revenue does. Everything else, depreciation, capex, interest, is small enough to skim for the large caps, which sit on net cash and hand most of it back to shareholders.
c4.read:
Two bar charts walk one hundred rupees of revenue down to what is left: large-cap outsourcers on the left, mid-cap specialists on the right. Read each left to right.

  • The first bar is the full hundred rupees.
  • Employee and subcontractor cost is the big bite. In the large-cap chart it takes a little under six of every ten rupees; in the mid-cap chart a little over six. That gap is scale and the pyramid: the giants run more juniors per senior and lean less on expensive subcontractors.
  • Travel, offices, sales and admin comes next. Mid caps spend a touch more here, because winning share from the giants costs sales effort.
  • Depreciation and interest is a sliver in both charts. That tiny bar is the asset-light model in one picture; set it beside a steel or telecom chart, where the same bar is enormous.
  • What is left lands in the low twenties for the large caps and the mid teens for the mid caps.

These are illustrative mid-cycle shapes, not any company's accounts; hover a bar for the amount.

Below the charts, the list marks which lines matter. Employee cost, utilisation and pyramid, and the rupee all get a yes: together they decide the margin. Receivables and working capital get a sometimes: they matter when a client is in trouble or work piles up unbilled. Depreciation, capex and interest get a no. When you read a results release, spend your time on the yes lines and skim the rest.

c5.story:
If you joined an Indian IT company in 2021, you probably juggled several offers, a joining bonus and a quick promotion. If you graduated in 2023, you may have waited the better part of a year for a joining date that kept slipping. Same companies, same campuses, two different worlds. That is the IT cycle, and it runs on Western boardroom budgets.

The boom was Covid's gift. Every company that had postponed going digital suddenly had no choice: banks needed apps, retailers needed e-commerce, everyone needed the cloud. Deal wins and hiring hit records, revenue grew in the mid to high teens, and the stocks traded at multiples usually reserved for consumer brands. By 2022 the boom was eating itself: engineers jumped jobs for big raises, attrition topped a fifth and margins got squeezed.

Then the bust. The US Federal Reserve raised rates at the fastest pace in decades, Silicon Valley Bank failed in March 2023, and discretionary spending froze. Growth sank to low single digits. ChatGPT, released in late 2022, added a new worry: what if machines write the code? In 2025 came tariffs, a steep new US fee on fresh skilled-worker visas, and the first big layoffs, with TCS cutting about one in fifty jobs.

Then, in early February 2026, after Anthropic released enterprise plugins for its Claude Cowork agent, the Nifty IT index had its worst single day since the Covid crash of March 2020. The fear was simple: if an agent can do the testing and the maintenance, who pays for the hours?

Which brings us to now: a long, flat bottom. Deal wins are steady, but mostly cost-cutting deals. Growth is flat. The companies remain hugely profitable and cash-rich, so the stocks have sagged rather than collapsed. The Q2 FY27 results showed the split: Tech Mahindra and HCLTech held up, while Wipro lagged on revenue and deal wins and leaned on a large buyback to reward shareholders.
c5.read:
Three pieces work together: the clock, the timeline and the four hands.

The clock splits into four arcs, boom, peak, bust and bottom, clockwise from the top. The years under each arc are the last cycle: boom from 2020 to 2022, peak in 2022, bust from 2023 to 2025, and a bottom spanning 2025 and 2026. The arrow points into the bottom arc, labelled a long, flat bottom. Notice how long the bust and bottom together run compared with the boom: the down-leg has outlasted the up-leg, which is the AI question showing up in the calendar.

The timeline retells it year by year from 2019. Boom years carry the boom colour, bust years the bust colour, and the 2026 entry is marked now. Notice that 2023 and 2025 are both coloured bust while 2024 is neutral: the downturn came in two waves, rates first, then tariffs, visas and AI.

The four hands let you move the arrow yourself:

  • Constant-currency growth: low single digits, flat. The hand to watch above all.
  • Deal wins and book-to-bill: steady but cost-cutting heavy, a mixed reading. Big deals become revenue in two to four quarters, at thinner prices.
  • Headcount and fresher hiring: flat to falling, a down arrow. Hiring is the most honest forecast a company makes.
  • The rupee: weak, an up arrow, because it props margins.

Look at the pattern: the only hand pointing up is the currency. Every hand that describes demand is flat, mixed or down. That is what a bottom without a catalyst looks like, and why the so-what line tells you to wait for discretionary spending before paying up.

c6.story:
An Indian IT company's quarter is decided by a cast of people who may never have visited Bengaluru. A finance chief at a Midwestern insurer trimming next year's technology budget. A Federal Reserve governor in Washington. A currency trader in Mumbai. A product manager in San Francisco shipping an agent that writes test scripts in seconds.

Three dials carry the most weight. The first is the health of the US economy and corporate profits, because that sets client budgets. When American companies are flush, they green-light the discretionary projects, the new apps and platforms, that carry the best prices. The second is the rupee, which sets margin: every bit of rupee weakness against the dollar flows almost straight into profit. The third is new and two-faced: AI adoption. Coding assistants and agents shrink the hours needed for old work like testing and maintenance, which deflates revenue now, but they also create a new pile of work, wiring AI into messy enterprises, that may arrive later. Nobody yet knows which effect wins, which is why this dial carries a diamond rather than an arrow.

Behind them sit the second-rank dials. US interest rates matter because rate hikes squeeze bank and tech budgets first, and those are the biggest clients. US bank earnings are a direct read on the largest vertical. Europe's economy, and its car industry in particular, drives the second-largest region and much of engineering R&D. Visa policy is two-faced too: a costlier visa raises the cost of onsite staff, but it also pushes work offshore, which is where Indian firms make their best margins.

One dial sets the revenue, one sets the margin, and the third is still deciding whose side it is on.

The small dials, Indian wage inflation and US tariffs, nudge rather than steer. And the Nifty IT index is less a cause than a thermometer: the market's own running verdict on where demand is heading.
c6.read:
Each row is one dial. Read across: the dial, the channel it travels through, what a rise does, how much it matters, and today's reading where we track a series.

  • The channel column is the most useful: it tells you which line of the results to look at. Client budgets means revenue; dollar revenue, rupee cost means margin.
  • The arrow on what a rise does: green up means a rise helps, red down means it hurts, a diamond means it cuts both ways. Mind the rupee row: the dial is the dollar against the rupee, so a rise, which is a weaker rupee, shows green.
  • The dots give the weight, one to three.

Scan the three-dot rows first. There are three: the US economy and corporate profits, the rupee, and AI adoption. Two can be read from public data. The third has no series and a diamond, and it is the one the market is most nervous about.

Then look at which rows show a live reading. The US ten-year yield, the rupee, the Nifty IT index and Indian consumer inflation map to series we track, and the last column gives the latest value and its date. The rest, US profits, AI, visas, bank earnings, Europe and tariffs, show a dash; you read those from the news and from the clients' own earnings calls.

Notice the colour balance too: most rows are green or mixed and only three are red, US rates, Indian wages and tariffs. This is an industry that does well when the West does well. The so-what line boils the whole table down to two dials: Western technology budgets set revenue, the rupee sets margin.

c7.story:
For two decades the pitch for Indian IT was simple: the same work, done well, at a fraction of Western cost, with a bottomless supply of engineers. The bottlenecks on this card are the places where that pitch is wearing thin, and the first two are new.

The first is AI deflation. The bread and butter of the large caps is unglamorous: testing, maintenance, application support, the work of keeping old systems running. That is exactly what coding assistants and agents are best at. A client who watches a tool write test scripts in seconds will not keep paying a team to write them by hand; at renewal, it asks for the savings. Revenue per project shrinks even when the client is perfectly happy.

The second is the captive centre. Walk around Bengaluru's tech parks and you will see Goldman Sachs, Walmart and Target on their own buildings. Global firms now run their own capability centres in India, hiring from the same colleges, sometimes poaching the same managers, and pulling in-house work that used to be outsourced. The labour arbitrage still exists; the client simply keeps it.

The cost advantage has not gone. It has started to change hands.

Then the recurring and cyclical irritants. US visa fees and outsourcing bills come back every few election cycles. Banking concentration means one scare, like the regional bank failures of 2023, freezes spending across the whole sector at once. Talent churn flips with the cycle: brutal in a boom, benign in a bust.

Finally the slow and the two-sided. The giants are now so large that only mega-deals move their growth, and mega-deals are mostly cost-cutting at thin prices. And engineering services depend on a handful of carmakers: when VinFast, the Vietnamese electric-vehicle maker, ran into trouble, Tata Technologies felt it for a whole year. Concentration cuts both ways: deep relationships when things go well, a single point of failure when they do not.
c7.read:
Each row is a bottleneck, why it bites, and a severity label. The label tells you where the risk belongs in your thinking.

  • Structural: AI deflation and captive centres. Both are permanent and both are new since the last decade. They belong in your valuation: a lower growth ceiling deserves a lower multiple or a higher payout, which is exactly what the so-what line says.
  • Recurring: visas and protectionism. A headline risk that returns every few years; it moves stocks for days and margins for a quarter or two.
  • Cyclical: banking concentration and talent churn. These bite at particular points on the clock, banking in a bust, churn in a boom. Use card five to tell which is live; today it is the banking side, not churn.
  • Slow: mature giants growing slowly. Not a shock but a gradient, and it explains why mid caps can outgrow large caps for years.
  • Two-sided: auto concentration in engineering R&D, a strength in good years and a weakness in bad ones.

Read the table top to bottom and notice the ordering. The two structural rows come first because they change the sector's long-run arithmetic; the rest is familiar weather that Indian IT has survived before. When you hear a bullish case for the sector, ask which of the first two rows it answers. If it answers neither, it is a cyclical case, and should be priced like one.

c8.story:
Indian IT is one of the least regulated big industries in India and one of the most exposed to other countries' politics. Almost every rule that can move its margins is written in Washington or Brussels.

Start with the US skilled-worker visa, the H-1B. For decades Indian firms used it to put engineers at client sites, and every few years it becomes an election-season punching bag. In September 2025 Washington slapped a steep new fee on fresh petitions. The immediate effect was a cost shock for anyone who relied on flying new engineers onsite. The second-order effect is subtler and partly positive: it pushes more work offshore to India, where margins are better, and nudges firms to hire locally in the US, which most large caps had been doing for years anyway. Then there are the proposed US outsourcing taxes, bills that would tax payments to foreign service providers. None has passed, but each new one filed is a headline that knocks the sector for a day.

At home, the big change was India's new labour codes, in force from November 2025. They redefined wages for gratuity and social security, which forced companies to book one-time charges in Q3 FY26 and adds a little to employee cost every year after. The data protection law and its rules are a compliance cost, but also a new line of work: helping clients comply.

For Indian IT, the most important regulator sits in Washington and does not answer to anyone in Delhi.

Europe matters through GDPR, the AI Act and data-transfer rules, which decide how much European work can be done from India at all. And then the slow-moving tax rules: transfer-pricing disputes over how profit is split between Indian and foreign arms, and the expiry of old SEZ tax holidays, which has nudged effective tax rates up over the years.

The odd one out is government procurement and production-linked incentives for servers and telecom gear. Irrelevant to TCS, decisive for the hardware door.
c8.read:
Each row is a rule or regulator: what it does, why you care, and a status tag. Use the status column to prioritise.

  • Live: US visa rules and fees, EU data and AI rules, and government procurement with production-linked incentives. These shape costs and orders now. The visa row is the one most likely to make headlines; the procurement row matters only for the hardware names.
  • Coming: proposed US outsourcing taxes. A single row, but the one with the biggest potential hit, because it would land on margins directly. Treat it as a tail risk to monitor, not a base case.
  • New: India's labour codes and the data protection law. The labour-code charge has already been taken; what remains is a small ongoing cost. The data law is both a cost and an opportunity.
  • Always: transfer pricing, and the SEZ and STPI regimes. Background noise that now and then produces a one-off tax charge.

Notice the split by geography. The rows that can move margins by more than a sliver are American: visas and outsourcing taxes. The Indian rows are mostly one-time adjustments or slow drifts. That tells you where to point your news alerts: Washington first, Brussels second, Delhi third, unless you own a hardware name, in which case Delhi's procurement calendar is everything.

Dated regulatory news for this industry, filtered from our feed, sits on the Picks and signals tab.

c9.story:
Indian IT is a strange case for Michael Porter's five forces. On paper it is a wonderful business: no factories, no debt, returns on capital most industries would envy, and most of the profit paid back to shareholders. So why does the market treat it as a business under pressure? Because forces that used to sit quietly have started pushing.

Start with buyers. A global bank does not hand its technology to one vendor. It runs a formal procurement, splits work across several Indian firms and Accenture, renegotiates every few years and, increasingly, writes AI savings into the contract: if your tools make the work faster, the bank wants its cut. That is buyer power with a spreadsheet.

Then rivalry. For a mega-deal the shortlist is nearly always the same: the big Indian names plus Accenture and Cognizant. They know each other's pricing, hire from the same colleges and bid hard for the cost-cutting deals that dominate today. Mid caps face less of this because they fight in narrower niches, insurance platforms or banking software, where the giants are less focused.

Substitutes are the force that changed most. AI tools, software-as-a-service products that replace custom-built systems, and the client's own captive centre all do some of what used to be outsourced. That is three substitutes at once, and all three are growing.

Where the large caps still look strong is suppliers and entrants. The suppliers here are engineers: in a boom they gain power and wages jump, in a bust they lose it. The giants, with training campuses and brand, feel this less than smaller firms. And entering this business at scale is genuinely hard; a record of decades without losing a bank's data is not something a start-up can buy. The only serious new entrant is the captive centre.

It is still a great business. It is just no longer one where nobody is coming for the surplus.
c9.read:
The radar has five spokes, one per force. The further a shape reaches along a spoke, the more pressure that force applies, so a smaller shape is the better business.

Two shapes are drawn: large-cap outsourcers, and mid caps with engineering services. The mid-cap shape is a neat, even pentagon, the same moderate pressure on every spoke. The large-cap shape is lopsided: it pokes further out on rivalry, buyers and substitutes, and pulls in tighter on suppliers and entrants.

So the shapes cross, and that is the interesting part.

  • Where the large caps reach further, rivalry, buyers and substitutes, size becomes a liability. The giants sell to the biggest, toughest buyers, meet the same rivals on every mega-deal, and do the most of the old work AI is replacing.
  • Where the large caps pull in, suppliers and entrants, size is a shield: they hold on to talent better, and nobody can easily copy their scale.

The table beside the chart gives each score from zero to three with its reason. Notice that nothing reaches three: this is not a bad business on any single force, just one under moderate pressure all round, with the large caps under heavier pressure on the forces that are growing.

The so-what line draws the conclusion: large caps keep healthy margins and pay most of it out, but share-gaining mid caps keep more of each extra rupee of profit. If you think AI's threat is overstated for a particular company, shrink its substitutes spoke in your head and watch how much better the shape looks.

c10.story:
An Indian IT results day is a blizzard: a press release, a fact sheet with dozens of tables, a deal-wins slide, an analyst call that runs well past an hour. Most of it is texture. Eight numbers tell you whether the quarter was good, and you can read them before the call starts.

Begin with constant-currency revenue growth. Reported growth gets pushed around by the euro and the pound, so companies also show growth as if exchange rates had not moved. That is real demand. Then the operating margin, which bundles pricing, utilisation and the rupee into one number. Read the two together: margin up with growth flat is usually the currency or a hiring freeze, not a better business.

Next, the pipeline. The total contract value of deal wins, set against quarterly revenue, gives book-to-bill. Above one means the company signed more than it billed, so the future is filling. But ask what kind of deals: a cost-cutting mega-deal looks wonderful on the slide and carries a thin price.

Then the people numbers, because people are the whole cost base. Employee cost to revenue tells you whether wage hikes or subcontractors are eating margin. Attrition and net headcount tell you two things at once: how much wage pressure is coming, and what management really expects, since nobody hires ahead of demand they do not believe in.

Read the headcount line before the guidance line. Hiring is the forecast management cannot spin.

Finally the quality checks. Days sales outstanding, including work done but not yet billed, warns of a client in trouble or a dispute. Return on capital confirms the asset-light model still works. And the payout ratio, dividends plus buybacks against free cash flow, is the number that has held the stocks up through a flat bottom. Wipro's buyback alongside soft Q2 FY27 numbers is the textbook case.
c10.read:
The table has eight rows: the number, what it tells you, what good looks like, and today's industry median from listed companies' latest annual filings.

  • What it tells you is the question each number answers. Ask it of every company you follow.
  • What good looks like is the only column with figures. Several rows give separate marks for large caps and mid caps; a margin that would be weak for TCS can be healthy for a mid cap.
  • Today's median is where the typical listed company sits. Three rows, deal-win contract value, attrition and headcount, and payout ratio, show a dash, because they come from company fact sheets and press releases rather than the annual filings we hold. Read those on results day.

Two caveats on the medians. The growth median is reported revenue growth, not constant currency, so it carries currency effects. The margin median is EBITDA margin, which sits a little above the operating margin the good column describes, because it is before depreciation; in IT the gap is small, but compare like with like.

Remember also that the median spans the whole industry, hardware names and small firms alongside the giants, so it will usually sit below the large-cap marks. The useful comparison for any company is three-way: its own number, the median, and the good mark for its tier. A company beating the median on growth while holding its margin through a flat bottom is the kind that leads the next up-cycle.

c11.story:
The best early warnings about Indian IT come from outside India, and they arrive on a timetable you can put in your diary.

The first voice is Accenture. Its fiscal quarters end a few weeks before the Indian companies' quarters do, so it reports first, and its bookings in consulting and discretionary work are the cleanest read on what Western clients are willing to start. The second voice is the US banks and Big Tech, whose earnings calls describe their technology budgets; budgets set this quarter become Indian revenue the next. Europe's car industry outlook does the same job for engineering services.

Further out, two quarters ahead, sit the slower signals: the US purchasing managers' index and corporate profits, which shape client confidence; the large deals announced today, which ramp up over two to four quarters; and fresher hiring and campus offers, because companies hire ahead of demand they believe in. The rupee is the odd one out: it speaks in the same quarter, straight to the margin.

Put the strongest signals together and you get the rule. The industry is in a real up-cycle when three things are true at once: constant-currency growth is accelerating, discretionary deals are rising alongside cost-cutting ones, and net hiring has restarted. Today none of the three is ticking. Growth is flat in low single digits, cost-cutting deals still dominate, and headcount is flat to falling. By the rule's own definition, the industry is still at the bottom.

No ticks out of three is not a crash signal. It is a patience signal.

Hence the call: prefer mid caps winning share and large caps with high cash payouts, and do not pay cycle multiples until discretionary spending returns. Stocks can still do fine at a bottom, through payouts and share gains, but a sector-wide re-rating needs the ticks.

The lead-time chart places each outside signal by how far ahead it speaks. The further right a dot sits, the earlier the warning.

  • Same quarter, far left: the rupee alone. It tells you about this quarter's margin, not about demand.
  • One quarter ahead: US bank and Big Tech calls, Accenture's bookings and the European car outlook. This is the busiest and most practical cluster: the reports to read in the weeks before Indian results.
  • Two quarters ahead: the US purchasing managers' index and profits, fresher hiring, and large deal announcements.
  • Three or more: empty for this industry. Nothing reliably speaks that far ahead, which is honest: IT demand turns on budget decisions made only a few months out.

Hover a dot to read its channel. Use the chart as a reading order: check the two-quarter dots first for direction, confirm with the one-quarter cluster, and treat the rupee as a margin adjustment.

Below the chart, the rule shows its three signs, all crossed today: growth flat, cost-cutting deals dominant, hiring flat to falling. The note beside each gives its current state. A sensible place to look for the first tick is discretionary deals, which show up early in Accenture's consulting bookings.

The call box gives the view, three points behind it and what would change it. Treat the would-change list as alerts: two quarters of accelerating growth, or US rate cuts that revive bank and tech spending, would argue for a turn, while a sharp rupee rally or a US outsourcing tax would hurt margins even with demand unchanged.
